cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(\mathrm{L}_{0}a_{1}\mathrm{L}_{1}\cdots a_{r} \mathrm{L}_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(\mathrm{L}_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(\mathrm{L}(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(\mathrm{L}(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.
cards.why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.

importance.reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.

cards.status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. Place–Zeitoun’s full-level-three decidability theorem remains distinct from the all-level target. The January 2025 alternation-hierarchy announcement is still explicitly withdrawn because of a fatal flaw in Lemma 19. No corrected result settling every fixed full dot-depth level was located.

context_blocks.text: Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA\)* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
cards.why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.

importance.reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.

cards.status_note: Primary-source review and a later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no decider or undecidability theorem for the unrestricted model stated here. The inspected 2025–2026 papers classify shape, growth or expressive power. Their claims do not decide ordinary functional equivalence of arbitrary pairs.

context_blocks.text: A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.

cards.title: Positivity problem for linear recurrences
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer \(d\ge 1\), integer initial values \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{d- 1}\), and integer coefficients \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{d- 1}\), halts and decides whether \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for every \(n\ge 0\), where \(u_{n+d}=\sum _{i=0}^{d- 1}a_{i} u_{n+i}\)? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
cards.definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from \(u_{0}\) onward and allows zero terms. Coefficients may be zero, including \(a_{0}\); the decision procedure must accept these inputs as well. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that nonnegativity of every term is decidable for integer linear recurrences of arbitrary input order, by a machine halting on both positive and negative instances, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. The property is \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for all \(n\ge 0\), including the initial values.
cards.why: A basic infinite-time safety question for finite linear descriptions. Its resolution would establish a major decidability boundary connecting verification, discrete dynamical systems and effective number theory, and would also settle general Skolem decidability.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.

progress.text: Ouaknine and Worrell establish positivity decidability through order five, and Diophantine consequences of extending it to order six.
For simple sequences, positivity is decidable through order nine.
Ultimate positivity is decidable for simple sequences of arbitrary order in PSPACE, and in polynomial time at each fixed order; this does not supply a general effective threshold.
Kenison, Nieuwveld, Ouaknine and Worrell establish positivity decidability for reversible sequences through order eleven, and simple reversible sequences through order seventeen.

The new survey retains general positivity as open and gives a concrete order-ten example whose positivity is unsettled. It also presents a reduction from order-five Skolem to positivity of simple order-ten sequences.

Low-order, simple-root, reversible and ultimate-positivity theorems have separate hypotheses and do not settle this arbitrary-order question.

context_blocks.text: A recurrence is a finite description of an infinite trajectory. One can compute any requested term exactly, but checking every term asks for a finite justification covering unbounded time. This makes positivity a basic test case for the limits of algorithmic verification. The July 2026 survey still lists its general decidability among the central unresolved problems. The word positivity is conventional here: the inequality is non-strict.

The connection to linear dynamics is direct. Store d consecutive values in a vector \(x_{n}\). A fixed integer companion matrix M then gives \(x_{n+1}=Mx_{n}\), and the first coordinate of \(M^{n} x_{0}\) is \(u_{n}\). The question is whether that coordinate ever enters the negative half-line. Even though the transition is linear and deterministic, the trajectory can combine growth, decay and oscillation through its characteristic roots.

No universal finite amount of simulation certifies the desired answer. For any chosen integer N, the sequence \(u_{n}=N- n\) satisfies \(u_{n+2}=2u_{n+1}- u_{n}\), is nonnegative through index N, and becomes negative afterward. Of course this particular family is easy to analyze. Its role is to distinguish sampling a long prefix from proving a bound that is computed from an arbitrary input and is sufficient for that input.

Ouaknine and Worrell decide positivity for all sequences of order at most five. Their analysis combines effective estimates from Diophantine approximation with decision procedures for real algebraic conditions. At order six, decidability would already imply that certain approximation constants associated with transcendental numbers are computable. This is a precise mathematical consequence, rather than a proof that no algorithm can exist.
Removing repeated characteristic roots improves the known frontier: positivity is decidable for simple sequences through order nine.

A separate theorem decides ultimate positivity for simple sequences of every order, in polynomial space. Ultimate positivity asks whether some finite prefix contains all negative terms. The algorithm need not provide an effective cutoff beyond which the terms are nonnegative. Without such a cutoff, the theorem cannot be turned into a positivity decider by checking the remaining prefix.

There are larger decidable orders under a different structural promise. An integer recurrence is reversible when its extension to all negative indices also has integer values. Kenison and coauthors decide positivity through order eleven for reversible sequences, and through order seventeen when they are also simple. The extra integrality in backward time matters; these bounds do not apply to arbitrary integer recurrences of those orders.

A general solution would also decide the Skolem problem, which asks whether an integer recurrence ever equals zero. Integer recurrence sequences are effectively closed under termwise products and subtraction of a constant. Thus \(w_{n}=u_{n}^{2}- 1\) is another such sequence, and it is nonnegative at every index exactly when u has no zero. Negating the answer to a positivity decider would decide Skolem. This reduction explains why positivity has consequences beyond sign analysis itself.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

importance.reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.

context_blocks.text: This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

cards.title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
cards.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
cards.definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.

importance.reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.

cards.status_note: The original question and the May 2026 two-level revision were rechecked on 11 September 2026. No construction in the specified theory T, or nondefinability theorem for T, was located. Results with outer strict equality or display primitives use additional structure and are recorded separately.

context_blocks.text: Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type \(A_{0}\) of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, \(A_{1}\) gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—\(A_{2}\) gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

cards.definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction \(\lambda x\).M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (\(\lambda x\).M)\(N=M[N/x]\), with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. \([D\to D]\) consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as \(\rho (x), MN\) as F(⟦M⟧\(\rho\))(⟦N⟧\(\rho\)), and \(\lambda x\).M as L(\(d\mapsto\)⟦M⟧\((\rho [x:=d])\)). The desired condition is \(\forall M,N\): (\(\forall \rho\), ⟦M⟧\(\rho\)=⟦N⟧\(\rho\)) ⇔ \(M=\beta N\). Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.

context_blocks.text: The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates \(\lambda x\).f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly \(\lambda \beta\) or \(\lambda \beta \eta\). They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly \(\lambda \beta\). Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.

cards.title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
cards.formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
cards.why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
cards.status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.

cards.definitions: S is a set of sorts, \(A\subseteq S\times S\) is a set of axioms, and \(R\subseteq S\times S\times S\) is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions \(t ::= x | s | t u | \lambda x:B\).\(t | \Pi x:B\).C, with \(s\in S\) and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) generated by the following rules. Axiom: \(\varnothing \vdash s:t\) when \((s,t)\in A\). Start: \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash x:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s\) and x is fresh. Weakening: \(\Gamma ,x:C\vdash t:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and x is fresh. Product: \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).\(C:s_{3}\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s_{1}, \Gamma ,x:B\vdash C:s_{2}\) and \((s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})\in R\). Abstraction: \(\Gamma \vdash \lambda x:B\).\(t:\Pi x:B\).C when \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).C:s for a sort s. Application: \(\Gamma \vdash t u:C[u/x]\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:\Pi x:B\).C and \(\Gamma \vdash u:B\). Conversion: \(\Gamma \vdash t:C\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and \(B=\beta C\). All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (\(\lambda x:B\).t)u to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =\(\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) for some finite \(\Gamma ,B\). Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.

sentences: A pure type system specifies a typed lambda calculus through a uniform collection of formation rules.
Weak normalization means that every well-typed term has some terminating reduction path.
The conjecture asks whether that global property forces every reduction path of every well-typed term to terminate.
A term may have both a normalizing route and a divergent route in less constrained rewriting settings, so the type-system hypothesis is essential.

context_blocks.text: A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let \(\Omega\)=(\(\lambda z\).zz)(\(\lambda z\).zz). The term (\(\lambda x\).y)\(\Omega\) reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce \(\Omega\) forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.

cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone \(\mathrm{NC}\ne\)monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size \(2^{n^{\Omega (1)}}\), improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.

context_blocks.text: Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.

cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
cards.why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.

importance.reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.

context_blocks.text: Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most \(n- 1\) scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc \((u,v)\) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes require \(n^{2- o(1)}\) space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.

cards.status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

cards.title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge 2, a\) uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
cards.why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.
cards.status_note: The original conjecture, primary distributed bounds, the 2025 locality result and the August 2026 resilient-LLL paper were checked on 11 September 2026. No result settling the exact bounded-degree \(O(\log  \log  n)\) worst-case target was found. The fixed factor \(1/2\) and order of slack/degree quantifiers preserve the saved precise interpretation. Node averages and results for stronger communication models are not substituted for this guarantee.
cards.review_note: User-approved research proposal, imported as a short draft. Its importance was assessed editorially; the full research-card standard has not yet been completed.

progress.text: Brandt and coauthors prove \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) lower bounds for sinkless orientation and distributed LLL under the stated criterion hypotheses.
Fischer–Ghaffari obtain \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  \log  n})}\) rounds at low dependency degree under polynomial slack and explicitly record the Chang–Pettie \(O(\log  \log  n)\) conjecture.
Davies gives \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) rounds under polynomially strengthened criteria, with a broader probability-versus-degree tradeoff.
Davies-Peck improves node-averaged LOCAL complexity and complexity in other models; Theorem 3 retains a separate, larger worst-case LOCAL bound.
Davies-Peck and Zhang extend efficient resilient-LLL applications to triangle-free coloring. Their general-degree discussion does not resolve the fixed-degree linear-log-log target.

cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.
