cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class \(H\subseteq \{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge 1\) admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying \(k+b\le Cd\), in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept \(h\in H\) is a total function \(X\to \{0,1\}\). A finite set \(A\subseteq X\) is shattered if \(\{h|_{A}:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{A}; d\) is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times \{0,1\}\) agreeing with some \(h\in H\). A scheme consists of deterministic maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\), which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable \(S, \kappa (S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\) is an unordered labeled subset with |\(T|\le k\) and \(z\in \{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor \(\rho (T,z):X\to \{0,1\}\) agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

progress.text: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions.

Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself.
Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open.

context_blocks.text: The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size \(2^{O(d)}\), settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size \(O(t \log (t+1))\) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate \(\eta\) with \(0<\eta <1/2\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret \(s\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), recovers s with probability at least \(2/3\) from independent samples \((a,\langle a,s\rangle \oplus e)\), where a is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and e is independently \(Bernoulli(\eta )\)?
cards.definitions: The inner product \(\langle a,s\rangle\) is \(\sum_{i} a_{i} s_{i}\) modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with \(\Pr [e=1]=\eta\). The learner knows n and the fixed rate \(\eta\), and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed \(\eta\) the algorithm and its polynomial bound \(p\eta\) may depend on \(\eta\), but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most \(p\eta (n)\) bit operations and requests at most \(p\eta (n)\) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational \(\eta\) does not demand a running-time bound uniform as \(\eta\) approaches \(1/2\) with n.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.

cards.status_note: The primary literature checked through 11 September 2026 leaves classical polynomial-time learning at fixed constant noise open. The card asks for all fixed rational rates separately, allowing rate-dependent polynomial bounds. The September 2026 reduction is conditional; sparse, quantum-example and limited-memory models do not replace the specified problem.

context_blocks.text: A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability \(1- \eta\). Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the \(2^{n}\) candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At \(\eta =1/4\), for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement \(3/4\), while every incorrect parity has expected agreement \(1/2\). A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a \(2^{O(n/\log  n)}\)-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) examples for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). The resulting running time is \(2^{O(n/\log  \log  n)}\). This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either \(\Omega (n^{2}/(1/2- \eta ))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed \(\eta\), the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by \(b\oplus \langle a,r\rangle\), learn the masked secret \(s\oplus r\) and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n, 2^{k}\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), with uniform-distribution error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(0\le k\le n, a k\)-junta is a function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) for which there is an unknown set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}, |S|\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that \(f(x)=g\)(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer \(t\ge 3\), setting \(\varepsilon =1/t\). Each requested example consists of an independently uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) and its exact, noiseless label \(f(x)\). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least \(2/3\) over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that \(h(x)\ne f(x)\) is at most \(1/t\). One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most \((n+2^{k}+t)^{C}\) steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.

cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

importance.reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.

progress.text: Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio publish the first constant-factor improvement over the brute-force exponent for learning arbitrary juntas from uniform examples.

context_blocks.text: A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of \(2^{k}\) is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with \(2^{k}\) entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about \(n^{k}\) possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most \((k+1)n^{k}\cdot 2^{2^{k}}\) juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that \(O((2^{k}+k \log (n+1)+\log (k+1)+1)/\varepsilon )\) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most \(\varepsilon\), with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately \(n^{0.704k}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(n,2^{k})\) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and \(2^{k}\), through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, \(f(x)=x_{1} \mathrm{XOR} x_{2} \mathrm{XOR} x_{3}\) is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and \(2^{k}\) is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most \(2^{k}\). Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class \(F_{k}\) of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^{k},1/\varepsilon )\) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when \(k=O(\log  n); a\) learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. Conditional hardness allowed as an outcome in the source is also weaker than an unconditional negative answer here. The source record is consolidated as a related milestone, not asserted to be an equivalent formulation; The removed TCS-0023 keeps its reserved ID and deletion reason; its bibliography and weaker milestone are preserved here.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every \(n,s\ge 1\), every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and all accuracy and confidence parameters \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n,s,1/\varepsilon\) and \(\log (1/\delta )\)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
cards.definitions: A literal is a variable \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form \((\mathrm{DNF})\) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers \(t,b\ge 2\) and set \(\varepsilon =1/t\) and \(\delta =2^{- b}\). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(p(n,s,t,b)\) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair \((x,f(x))\) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least \(1- \delta\) over the examples and internal randomness, \(\Pr_{x\text{ drawn from }D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\). Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

context_blocks.text: A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most \(3^{n}\) simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by \((3^{n}+1)^{s}\). The finite-class union bound therefore gives \(O((ns+\log (1/\delta ))/\varepsilon )\) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical \(n^{O(s)}\) algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound \(2^{\widetilde{O} (n^{1/3} \log  s)}\). For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most \(2^{k}\) terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.

cards.why: Determine whether compact Boolean rules that need only polynomially many observations can also be learned with polynomial computation, without assumptions on the input distribution. A positive result would cover decision trees and uniform-example juntas; a negative result would identify a fundamental computational barrier in realizable learning even when the output representation is unrestricted.

cards.title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
cards.why: This asks whether the simplest intersection of linear classification rules remains efficiently learnable from ordinary examples under arbitrary distributions. A positive answer would remove a distributional assumption from a central margin-learning model; a negative answer would establish a computational obstruction even when the learner may use any efficiently evaluable representation.

cards.definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.

context_blocks.text: A single separating hyperplane with a margin is a basic tractable classification model. Intersecting two such regions is already a substantial test of distribution-independent learning: allowing an arbitrary output hypothesis removes the requirement to recover two separating hyperplanes themselves.

Diakonikolas, Ma, Ren and Tzamos obtain an efficient learner when the distribution factors between the span of the two normal vectors and its orthogonal complement. Their general-model discussion on printed page 1473 leaves the distribution-free margin problem unresolved. The factorization promise is an additional assumption, not a consequence of a geometric margin.

A July 2026 revision by Alman, Patel and Servedio reports subexponential-time distribution-free learning for Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces. That running time does not meet the polynomial bound asked here.

A separate July 2026 revision by Patel and Vempala reports a margin-sensitive algorithm for intersections of a variable number of halfspaces. Its abstract does not establish a polynomial-time learner for two halfspaces; its discussion of matching lower bounds cannot be transferred to the fixed-two case without checking their parameter range.

A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

context_blocks.text: Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant \(c>0\), all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
cards.definitions: \(U_{n}\) is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output \(f(x)\), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real \(c>0\) there exists \(N(I,c)\) such that the inequality holds for every \(n\ge N(I,c)\). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

importance.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

progress.text: The theory of computational cryptography develops reductions from one-way functions. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby establish equivalence between existence of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.
Bogdanov and Trevisan give a nonadaptive oracle-reduction barrier to basing average-case NP hardness or one-way security on NP-complete worst-case hardness, unless PH collapses.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.9 explicitly asks whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) implies one-way functions, and separately asks about stronger average-case premises and trapdoor conclusions. This card fixes the basic one-way-function implication.

Liu and Pass strengthen characterizations using boundary hardness of randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. Their ordinary deterministic \(K^{t}\) consequence assumes exponential circuit hardness for derandomization; it does not derive one-way functions from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the original source. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no derivation of eventually secure classical one-way functions from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone was located. The security quantifiers are stronger than an infinitely-often one-wayness target.

context_blocks.text: If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

Cryptographic one-way functions require a stronger kind of difficulty: efficient attackers must fail to invert outputs generated from random inputs.
This project asks whether worst-case hardness alone forces that average-case cryptographic hardness to exist.
A function that is hard only on an extremely rare set would not provide the required security.
Resolving the implication would clarify whether the most familiar complexity assumption already contains the foundations of computational cryptography.

cards.context:
If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

benchmark_focus.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix \(q(n)\) to be the least prime at least \(n^{4}\) for every integer \(n\ge 2\). Let \(\chi _{n}\) be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to \(\exp (- \pi e^{2}/n^{2})\). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial \(m(n)\), the ensembles (\(A,A s+e\) mod q) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m\times n}, s\) is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{n}\), the m coordinates of e are independent \(\chi _{n}\) samples, and u is independent uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m}\). Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than \(n^{- c}\) eventually for every constant \(c>0\). No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in \(\lambda +|C|\) that outputs a Boolean circuit \(O(1^{\lambda},C)\) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible \(\mu _{p}\) such that for every |\(C|\le p(\lambda )\), with probability at least \(1- \mu _{p}(\lambda )\) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences \(C_{0},\lambda\) and \(C_{1},\lambda\) with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. The construction uses that stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.

cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
cards.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer \(c\ge 3\) and polynomial sample count \(M(d)\), let \(q(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^{c}\), let s be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{d}\), let A be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{M(d)\times d}\), and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp (- \pi z^{2}/(4d))\), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and \((A,u)\), for independent uniform \(u\in Z_{q}^{M(d)}\), are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{Z,2\sqrt{d}}\); only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\to\)(pk,evk,sk), \(Enc(pk,b)\), Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by \(\mathrm{P}(\lambda )\), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in \(\lambda\) and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most \(p(\lambda )\) and all input bits \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t}\), decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals \(C(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t})\), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than \(\lambda ^{-a}\) eventually for every \(a>0\). No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.

importance.reason: A central foundational gap in fully homomorphic encryption, separating established leveled LWE constructions from reusable fixed-depth-independent keys and their extra security assumptions.

progress.text: Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan establish leveled FHE from ordinary LWE; the journal abstract explicitly separates the additional weak circular-security assumption for removing levels.
Brakerski’s quantum-FHE paper records a classical bootstrappable GSW-style scheme with polynomial modulus, citing Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan; this does not eliminate the separate key-cycle issue.
Micciancio’s slides pose the ordinary-LWE circular-security question and distinguish FHE from full composability.
Bitansky–Solomon bootstrap via functional encryption under polynomial hardness assumptions; extra primitives remain, and nonuniform security needs an additional complexity assumption.
Wang–Huang–Tang remove CRS and circularity assumptions in a dynamic multi-key construction whose formal setup still takes L.
Liu and coauthors’ quantum proposal retains \(\mathrm{L}+1\) key layers and a quantum evaluator, outside the target model.

cards.status_note: No classical unleveled compact FHE construction from the specified ordinary LWE assumption alone was found through 11 September 2026. Functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions. The inspected February and April 2026 no-circularity proposals retain explicit level bounds; the latter also uses quantum evaluation. This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

context_blocks.text: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer. Compactness makes this substantive: the client should decrypt a short answer, rather than receive the original ciphertexts together with the whole circuit and perform the computation itself. Here all four algorithms are classical, and the ciphertext for one output bit remains bounded by a fixed polynomial in the security parameter.

The order of choices is the heart of the problem. In a leveled scheme, the user first chooses a maximum depth L and generates keys suitable for that level. This can support every circuit up to L without revealing the data. The present question asks for one key-generation algorithm that receives only the security parameter and supports every polynomial-depth circuit later supplied to the evaluator. Choosing \(\mathrm{L}=\lambda ^{10}\) during setup still leaves deeper polynomial computations outside the guarantee.

Lattice ciphertexts generally include small errors that hide the plaintext. Homomorphic operations transform the desired message and these errors together. Once the error exceeds the decryption tolerance, the output may no longer decode correctly. Gentry’s bootstrapping idea refreshes a ciphertext by homomorphically evaluating a decryption circuit, with the secret key itself provided in encrypted form. Micciancio’s teaching slides explain both this noise issue and the associated circular-security question.

A chain of independent keys avoids the immediate circularity. Encrypt the secret key at level i under the public key at level \(i+1\), then use the next level to refresh the current ciphertext. The usual hybrid proof can replace those encryptions in reverse order because the chain has an endpoint. But the public material grows with the number of refreshes planned in advance. Closing the chain into a cycle reuses a bounded collection of keys and changes the security argument.

Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan’s construction makes the distinction explicit in its journal abstract: ordinary LWE gives leveled FHE, while removing the depth restriction uses an additional weak circular-security assumption. Later bootstrapping work supports polynomial-modulus parameters and polynomial lattice approximation factors. Improvements in error growth and efficiency do not themselves justify exposing the secret-key encryptions needed to reuse the keys.

The requested proof need not avoid bootstrapping, or even avoid encrypted keys. It must justify the actual public evaluation information using ordinary LWE alone. Conversely, it is not enough to prove that some artificially designed CPA-secure encryption scheme becomes insecure when encrypting its own key. Such a counterexample refutes an automatic upgrade for every scheme; it does not rule out designing a particular FHE scheme with a valid ordinary-LWE proof.

Bitansky and Solomon obtain FHE without circular-security assumptions using functional encryption, under polynomial hardness assumptions. This is a significant positive result for a broader assumption set. In their ITCS 2023 construction, the available functional-encryption instantiation uses assumptions including LPN, bilinear SXDH and shallow pseudorandom generators, in addition to the LWE-based homomorphic component. The basic theorem protects against uniform adversaries; their nonuniform extension requires an additional worst-case complexity assumption. Neither version establishes LWE alone under the convention here.

Recent claims also require checking the formal setup. Wang, Huang and Tang’s February 2026 dynamic multi-key scheme advertises avoiding a common reference string and circular security. Definition 2.2 nevertheless gives Setup the depth parameter L, and the construction chooses its dimension and modulus using L. Its stated compactness also permits dependence on L. This is a leveled guarantee, even though the number of participating keys can change dynamically.

Liu and coauthors’ April 2026 quantum homomorphic proposal also advertises classical LWE and no circular-security assumption. Its Section 3.4 uses \(\mathrm{L}+1\) independent key layers; a later discussion explicitly preallocates L evaluation gadgets. It therefore retains a level bound, and its evaluator performs quantum operations. These scope differences already prevent it from settling the classical, depth-independent target; this review does not validate its separate efficiency or quantum-security claims.

There is a further definitional distinction between evaluating one arbitrary circuit on fresh ciphertexts and repeatedly evaluating new circuits on the resulting ciphertexts. Micciancio’s slides show that correctness for the first task does not automatically imply correctness for the second. This card asks for the usual fresh-input FHE guarantee. Establishing full composability would be an additional accomplishment, rather than an implicit condition that makes the target harder.

A solution would remove a central gap between the clean assumption used to prove the security of leveled lattice encryption and the extra assumption used to reuse a fixed key set indefinitely over polynomial computations. It would clarify the foundation of FHE independently of practical parameter optimization, and could improve the assumptions of constructions that use unrestricted encrypted computation as a component.

cards.title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
cards.why: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Nir’s August 2026 ECCC report, Theorem 1.5, claims a general scheme with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\), directly implying the stated strict threshold after adjustment of the universal constant. cards.definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\). Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and \(1/2\) absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs \(\log _{2} M\), even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is \(1.5^{n+o(n)}\), equivalently \(2^{0.58496\ldots n+o(n)}\). This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy \(c<1/2\).

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.
