cards.title_en: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions

context_blocks.text: Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).

cards.context:
Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
cards.definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most \(1/3\) separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on \(1^{n}\) generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |\(x\rangle\), polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |\(0\rangle\), and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.

importance.reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.

progress.text: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\). Wigderson’s Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2 state the model and inclusion.
Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms. No unconditional classical polynomial-time lower bound for those tasks follows.
Raz and Tal prove an oracle separation \(\mathrm{BQP}\not\subset \mathrm{PH}\). This also separates BQP from BPP relative to that oracle, but not in ordinary unrelativized computation.
Bene Watts and Parham publish an unconditional shallow-circuit sampling separation. Its classical resource restrictions and sampling output differ from the unrestricted decision model fixed here.

cards.status_note: Wigderson’s Conjecture 11.4 explicitly asks for strict containment. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no unrelativized separation of these bounded-error decision classes was located. Oracle and shallow-circuit sampling advantages are recorded with their model restrictions.

context_blocks.text: Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\) would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every fixed local dimension \(q\ge 2\), interaction range \(r\ge 1\), interaction incidence bound \(g\ge 1\), norm bound \(J>0\), and spectral gap \(\Delta >0\), is there a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta )\) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), has unique ground state \(\psi\) satisfying \(S(\rho _{A})\le C|\partial A|\) for every \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(\mathrm{L}\ge 1\) be an integer, \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}=\{1,\ldots ,\mathrm{L}\}^{2}\) with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of \(C^{q}\) over its sites. Write \(H=\sum_{a} h_{a}\), where each \(h_{a}\) is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support \(X_{a}\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every \(h_{a}\) is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector \(\psi\) and its next eigenvalue is at least \(\Delta\) above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), let \(A^{c}\) be its complement in \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(\rho _{A}=Tr_{A^{c}}(|\psi \rangle \langle \psi |)\) and \(S(\rho _{A})=- Tr(\rho _{A} \log _{2} \rho _{A})\), with \(0 \log _{2} 0=0\). The boundary \(\partial A\) is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.

importance.reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.

progress.text: Hastings proves the area law for gapped one-dimensional quantum systems; the bound depends on fixed local parameters.
Huang establishes QMA-completeness of two-dimensional local Hamiltonian problems even when ground states satisfy area laws, without claiming a uniform spectral gap.
Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar publish an area law for entanglement spread, rather than von Neumann entropy.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset give a nearly linear entropy bound for vertical cuts in locally gapped frustration-free systems. In arXiv version 3, the explicit bound is \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) at the end of §4.
Arad, Firanko, and Jain extend approximate-projector methods to mutual information of maximally mixed ground states; their theorem still requires a good approximate ground-space projector.
Garratt and Abanin derive entropy bounds from thermodynamic information and area laws for frustration-free systems with suitably bounded subsystem ground-space degeneracies.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.

context_blocks.text: A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy \(m \log _{2} q\). For a square block of side length \(\ell\), that is proportional to \(\ell\)\(^{2}\), whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times \(\ell\). The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension \(q^{\mathrm{L}}\), which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol \((\mathrm{P},V)\) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let \(p(C)\) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have \(p(C)\ge 2/3\) and NO instances have \(p(C)\le 1/3\). V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]\(\ge 2/3\). On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]\(\le 1/3\). Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
cards.definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient quantum computation has an equally efficient, purely classical way to establish trust without computational hardness assumptions or isolated extra devices. A resolution would identify a basic boundary between producing quantum answers and certifying them.

importance.reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.

context_blocks.text: A user who can run only classical computations would like to check the answer returned by a quantum computer. Repeating the same claimed computation on the same untrusted device gives no independent reason to trust it. Interactive verification instead lets the user issue challenges whose answers constrain whether the reported result is correct. The survey by Gheorghiu, Kapourniotis and Kashefi organizes approaches according to what the verifier can do and which resources or assumptions establish trust. This card fixes the most restrictive physical verifier: entirely classical.

The usual inclusion \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}\) does not settle the question. Since quantum polynomial time is contained in polynomial space, Shamir’\(s \mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) theorem supplies a classical interactive proof with an unrestricted prover. However, a proof system whose honest prover must carry out much harder auxiliary computations cannot be implemented merely by running the quantum computation being certified. Requiring the honest prover to be quantum polynomial time is therefore substantive.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev show that a verifier with a small quantum register can verify arbitrary efficient quantum computations. Quantum authentication lets a weak client protect data while delegating its processing. This demonstrates that a very limited quantum capability can be enough, but its communication and trusted operations do not satisfy the all-classical interface specified here. Their 2017 paper supplies the completed journal treatment of work first reported in 2008.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani provide another route: a classical verifier interacts with separated quantum devices sharing entanglement. Correlations in nonlocal games can force the devices to implement the required states and measurements. Isolation is crucial because it prevents the devices from coordinating arbitrary answers during the test. Combining both devices into one freely communicating prover removes that constraint, so the multiprover result cannot simply be reused for this card.

Mahadev’s 2018 breakthrough gives classical verification with one efficient quantum prover under the hardness of Learning With Errors for quantum algorithms. Cryptographic structure conceals information needed to cheat in the measurement tests. Its soundness is computational: the theorem protects against efficiently implementable attacks under the assumption. The present question deliberately quantifies over unbounded cheating strategies, which may break the underlying cryptography.

Recent work continues to refine these neighboring models. Kalai, Khurana and Raizes’s February 2026 construction verifies computations using one reusable QMA witness without destroying it, with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE. This is useful when the input quantum state cannot be copied. It retains the computational soundness assumption and therefore does not supply an unconditional protocol for the simpler BQP target here.

Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier’s May 2026 journal article achieves information-theoretic verification without trusted state preparations or measurements. Its client still applies trusted quantum gates: one construction uses single-qubit Z rotations and bit flips. Removing two particular hardware requirements is meaningful progress, but a client performing these gates is not a purely classical verifier.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi explicitly retain the single-prover question in April 2026. They prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\subseteq MIP^{O}\) for every classical oracle O using an exponentially long classical proof queried in polynomially many locations. Their theorem concerns multiple classical provers and does not establish efficient honest provers. Relativization is proposed as a way to investigate the difficulty, rather than as an equivalence that resolves it.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Do there exist finite integers \(a,b\ge 2\) and a bipartite density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{a}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{b}\) such that \(\rho\) has negative partial transpose, but \(\langle \psi |(\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}})^{\otimes k}|\psi \rangle \ge 0\) for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\) of Schmidt rank at most two across \((\mathbb{C} ^{a})^{\otimes k}:(\mathbb{C} ^{b})^{\otimes k}\)?
cards.definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by \((\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}})_{ij,k\ell}=\rho _{i\ell ,kj}\). Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that \(\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}}\) has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is \(\psi\). Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs \((|00\rangle +|11\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

importance.reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.

cards.status_note: The all-copy NPT bound-entanglement question remains explicitly open in the July 2026 primary sources. New two-copy solutions and restricted three-copy progress do not settle this formulation. Reviewed through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(d,\alpha )=(I+\alpha F)/(d^{2}+\alpha d)\), where \(d\ge 3, - 1\le \alpha \le 1\) and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when \(\alpha <- 1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly when \(\alpha <- 1/2\). Consequently the interval −\(1/2\le \alpha <- 1/d\) consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for \(d\ge 3\). The endpoint \(\alpha =- 1/2\) is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. The distinction makes the remaining challenge concrete: control every admissible rank-two witness across the full collection of copies, rather than only witnesses with a convenient internal structure.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
cards.why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

context_blocks.text: A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space \(2^{N}\), with coordinates numbered \(0,1,\ldots\) and fair-coin product measure \(\mu\). For a finite binary string \(\sigma\), the cylinder \([\sigma ]\)={\(X:\sigma\) is a prefix of X} has measure \(2^{- |\sigma |}\). A Martin-Löf test is a sequence \((U_{k})_{k\ge 1}\) of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs \((k,\sigma )\), with \(U_{k}\) equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and \(\mu (U_{k})\le 2^{- k}\). A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test \(X\notin \bigcap _{k} U_{k}\). A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier \(q\in [0,2]\), before seeing \(X(j)\). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After \(X(j)\) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by \(2- q\) if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. \(q=1\) allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central equivalence problem for algorithmic randomness: determine whether adaptive computable prediction detects every failure of effective measure-theoretic randomness.

cards.status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

context_blocks.text: These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most \(1/R\). Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow define propositional proof-system efficiency and formalize the extension rule. Their equivalence theorems make EF polynomial boundedness independent of standard presentations; Cook’s posted correction to Corollary 4.7 keeps the coNP-versus-NP premise explicit.

Wigderson’s book lists superpolynomial unrestricted Frege lower bounds as open and distinguishes the additional sharing available in Extended Frege. Lower bounds for the weaker system would not automatically apply to EF.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) with additional formal provability hypotheses. The checked preprint does not give an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh, Jain, Li and Mathialagan construct succinct non-interactive arguments for NP under promise derandomization, LWE, SXDH and a bounded-arithmetic hardness-certification assumption. The formal unprovability premise differs from the unconditional proof-size target.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations and explicitly explains why it does not give a Frege or EF lower bound for propositional tautologies.

Akbar Tabatabai reports exponential separations between EF systems for intuitionistic substructural and linear logics. The preprint’s stated scope differs from this classical system; its proof was not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
cards.definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.
cards.why: This asks whether naming and reusing intermediate formulas can shorten rigorous propositional proofs by more than every polynomial factor. It is a central comparison between strong proof systems and between reasoning with formula trees and shared circuit representations. A separation would yield superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege; an equivalence would show that the extension rule changes shortest-proof lengths by at most polynomial factors.

Buss characterizes Frege size simulation of EF through polynomial-size partial EF consistency proofs in Frege, and proves polynomial-size partial Frege self-consistency proofs. The 2002 date on the downloadable typescript is not a new publication.

context_blocks.text: Frege proofs model a finite list of ordinary propositional deductions. Extended Frege adds named definitions, allowing a long expression to be referenced by a variable after paying for its definition. Chains of these definitions describe shared Boolean circuits. Every assignment to the ordinary variables extends uniquely through an acyclic sequence of definitions, so the extension rule preserves truth of conclusions that contain no extension variables. This explains the systems' common set of theorems while leaving their proof lengths potentially different.

Proof reuse and subformula sharing are different resources. Both systems may cite an earlier proof line many times; ordinary Frege still pays for every occurrence inside each newly written formula. Extended Frege also has names for intermediate expressions. This representational distinction does not itself show that any tautology lacks a short Frege proof. The question compares the best proofs available in the two systems, irrespective of how those proofs were discovered.

The usual robustness theorem compares finite sound and complete Frege presentations with polynomial overhead. Cook and Reckhow also define fresh extension variables and establish the analogous robustness of Extended Frege. The card preserves the saved size-simulation target while making its syntax and bit accounting explicit. It restores the source convention allowing auxiliary ordinary variables; restricting such variables to those of the conclusion gives a polynomially equivalent convention. A bounded-depth, tree-like or otherwise restricted Frege system would be a different question.

A polynomial bound on the existence of translated proofs is distinct from a polynomial-time translator. Buss's work separates these notions and relates size simulation to short finite consistency proofs. His 1991 result characterizes Frege simulation of Extended Frege by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the corresponding partial EF consistency statements: finite propositional assertions that a contradiction has no proof up to a specified length. Frege already has polynomial-size partial self-consistency proofs. This comparison is a stated theorem about the systems, not a resolution of Frege versus EF. The current review checked the author and publisher abstracts; the author's downloadable copy is headed 11 July 2002, although the journal publication is from 1991.

Buss's Stanford tutorial of 27 February 2014 explicitly presents the formula-versus-circuit proof comparison as a longstanding open question. Its discussion of proposed separating principles is historical context, not a current lower-bound theorem. Quasipolynomial upper bounds for particular families must remain distinct both from polynomial upper bounds and from a separation of the unrestricted systems.

A concrete example is the Kneser–Lovász coloring principle. The graph has the \(k\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) as vertices and joins disjoint subsets; for \(n\ge2k\), its propositional principle rules out a proper coloring with \(n-2k+1\) colors. Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs for each fixed \(k\). Constants and exponents may depend on that fixed parameter. Their 2015 conference version states these as Theorems 4 and 5; the 2018 expanded journal abstract retains the fixed-parameter condition. These are upper bounds for particular tautologies, not a superpolynomial Frege lower bound or a uniform bound with both parameters growing.

Krajíček's 11 June 2026 preprint describes circuit-equivalence reasoning by local circuit rewrites. Its relation is polynomial-time recognizable, and each rewrite may delete gates and add at most seven; a short EF proof yields a polynomially bounded chain. The intermediate objects retain circuit sharing. The concluding discussion also distinguishes existence of a small chain from a polynomial-time construction of it by the presented proof. This normal-form statement therefore supplies neither the polynomial-size formula proof nor the polynomial-time translator that could be mistakenly inferred from the abstract.

The September 2026 report by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay states a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted Ideal Proof System over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), the field with two elements. Certificates are algebraic formulas. The original variables are divided into two groups, noncommuting within a group and commuting across groups; Definition 1.1 separately specifies the noncommuting placeholder variables and included Boolean and commutator axioms. Theorem 1.2 concerns refutations of unsatisfiable CNFs in that model. Its certificate restrictions and quasipolynomial overhead both prevent it from answering the unrestricted EF question. The report and theorem scope were checked; its complete new proof was not independently verified.

An EF proof includes its final formula, so a superpolynomial separation from Frege would imply superpolynomial Frege proof-size lower bounds as a function of formula length. The converse need not follow: a family hard for Frege might also require long EF proofs. Likewise, the separate question whether EF is polynomially bounded asks whether every tautology has a short EF proof, rather than whether Frege can match EF's shortest proofs. The present card makes no assumption that \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) and does not identify a computation-class separation with this proof-system comparison.
