context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a \(1/q\) fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below \(1/q\) is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.

cards.title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), determine the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. Give a real-valued function \(g\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The tolerance is absolute in the competitive ratio and is the same for every \(k\).
cards.definitions:
A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify an unambiguous function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[\forall k\ge1,\quad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le1/100.\]
Both sides of the error interval must be proved with the metric, rule, additive-constant and sequence quantifiers above. In particular, certified functions \(\ell,u\) satisfying \(\ell(k)\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u(k)\) and \(u(k)-\ell(k)\le1/50\) for every positive integer \(k\) qualify through their midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. An upper bound on an infimum must not silently be replaced by existence of a rule attaining its endpoint.

The absolute error must remain at most \(1/100\) as \(k\) grows; relative error \(k/100\), a constant-factor asymptotic estimate, or finitely many solved server counts does not meet it. A rule for a particular metric family or one named algorithm establishes only the corresponding restricted guarantee. A lower bound must rule out all allowed deterministic rules on its witnessing metric, rather than only one proposed algorithm or proof certificate. No unproved additional hypothesis is part of the target. There is no fixed formula grammar or polynomial evaluation requirement for \(g\), but repeating the defining infimum without determining its value is not an answer. The benchmark precision does not assert the classical exact equality \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) or endpoint attainment.
cards.why: The k-server problem measures the movement cost of responding to demand without knowing future requests. It includes paging and serves as a basic problem in competitive analysis, with the same number of resources available to the online rule and the offline optimum.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The April 2026 benchmark explicitly retains the deterministic conjecture, and the inspected July 2026 ICALP paper retains the classical general bound while studying randomized computational efficiency. Bounded searches found no full matching solution claim or determination of the universal infimum function within absolute 1/100 for all k. The 2025 time-model lower bound, 2023 randomized disproof and 2026 advice/randomness results have different scopes. This card retains the earlier explicit numerical reformulation; exact k-competitiveness, equality of the infimum, and approximation at the benchmark tolerance are distinct claims. Current-source checks are bounded and do not constitute independent certification of the literature.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. Combined with the lower bound, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The classical conjecture predicts an actual \(k\)-competitive rule for every metric. Such rules would imply \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\). Knowing only this infimum value would establish rules arbitrarily close to \(k\), without by itself establishing endpoint attainment. Likewise, an approximation within the benchmark's absolute \(1/100\) tolerance may leave the exact equality undecided.

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. cards.context:
On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. Combined with the lower bound, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The classical conjecture predicts an actual \(k\)-competitive rule for every metric. Such rules would imply \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\). Knowing only this infimum value would establish rules arbitrarily close to \(k\), without by itself establishing endpoint attainment. Likewise, an approximation within the benchmark's absolute \(1/100\) tolerance may leave the exact equality undecided.

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. It explicitly distinguishes passing those finite checks from a proof covering all configurations and request sequences. Its reported experiments do not resolve the remaining general case.

Its reduction uses few random bits, but does not eliminate randomness. A separate deterministic consequence supplies advice that depends on the instance. cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, determine the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(L(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. Approximate \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\), with a complete Lean proof. No complexity hypothesis is included in the definition of this number.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance. The numerical tolerance applies to this infimum, not to the feasibility or objective guarantee of a proposed schedule.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify a real value \(a\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[|a-\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}|\le\frac1{100}.\]
Both sides of the claimed error interval must be certified for the full deterministic polynomial-bit-time model above. In particular, proved bounds \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualify through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\); exact determination also qualifies. Upper and lower bounds must have the infimum quantifiers specified above, without silently requiring attainment or substituting a fixed machine count. An unambiguous mathematical expression or certified specification of \(a\) is acceptable without a decimal expansion, but simply restating the defining optimization is not a determination. A one-sided algorithmic improvement or relaxation gap alone does not meet the criterion.

No unproved complexity assumption is implicit in this target. A theorem proved only under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is a conditional bound, not an unconditional certification of this number. An answer expressed by cases must establish the required error bound in every case. Here \(\mathrm P\) denotes languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines and \(\mathrm{NP}\) languages having polynomial-length witnesses verified in polynomial time. The \(1/100\) allowance is benchmark precision on the ratio; it need not decide whether the exact infimum equals two.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The SODA 2024 source explicitly leaves the unrestricted constant improvement unresolved; the inspected 2026 prediction, fair-mechanism and knapsack literature does not give an algorithm for the full model here. Bounded searches found no determination of the infimum within absolute 1/100 or full matching solution claim. The known 3/2 lower bound assumes P differs from NP, while the quantity itself is unconditional. The tolerance target is an explicitly retained editorial reformulation; neither an old open-question statement nor absence of a search result independently certifies its current openness.

context_blocks.text: The original source question asks whether some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), independent of the instance, permits a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation. The user-authorized quantitative reformulation of 12 September 2026 instead asks for the full infimum of achievable ratios with absolute \(1/100\) benchmark precision. This broader quantity retains the original scheduling model. An approximation to that quantity can satisfy the benchmark while leaving the exact below-two threshold unanswered.

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.

Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

importance.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

progress.text: Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov obtain polynomial-time recovery for every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with a polynomial exponent that can depend on that constant.

The final gradient-descent preprint proves recovery at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt n\) from full-graph initialization, for each fixed desired error probability.

cards.status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given \(1^{n}\), halts within \(q(n)\) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution \(D_{n}\) is over finite binary strings \(x; |x|\le q(n)\), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives \((1^{n},x)\), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write \(T_{A}(1^{n},x)\) for its running time. The pair \((\mathrm{L},D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an \(A, \varepsilon >0, C>0\), and integer \(k\ge 1\) with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every \(n\ge 1\). The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

cards.status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |\(x|^{2}- 1\) further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree \(\Delta\) and every integer \(q\ge \Delta +2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(n\ge 1\) and \(\Omega\)={\(\sigma :V(G)\to [q] : \sigma (u)\ne \sigma (v)\) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from \(V(G)\), then choose a colour uniformly from \([q]\)\\(\{\sigma (u):u\in N(v)\}\) and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega\). Define \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min \{t\in Z_{\ge 0}: \max _{\sigma \in \Omega} (1/2)\sum_{\tau \in \Omega}|\mathrm{P}^{t}(\sigma ,\tau )- \pi (\tau )|\le 1/4\}\). This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of \(n, \Delta , q\) and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central boundary question for Markov-chain sampling: does the simplest local recolouring process mix efficiently whenever the universal ergodicity threshold is met?

importance.reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general-graph \(\Delta +2\) conjecture remains open in the checked sources. August 2026 results improve restricted-girth regimes with fixed relative slack; they do not establish the universal additive-two bound.

context_blocks.text: A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold \(\Delta +2\) has a concrete role. On a clique with \(\Delta +1\) vertices and exactly \(\Delta +1\) colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least \(\Delta +2\) colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and \(q/(q- \Delta )\). That factor is at most \(1+\Delta /2\) in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’\(s q>2\Delta\) regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly \(11\Delta /6\). The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the \(11/6\) threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains \(\Delta +2\) as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes \(\Delta \ge 125\) and \(q\ge 1.809\Delta\) and proves \(O(n \log  n)\) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal \(O(n \log  n)\) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on \(\Delta\) and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves \(n^{O(\operatorname{tw}(G)^{3})}\) mixing with \(q\ge \Delta +2\), so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses \(q\ge (1+\varepsilon )(\Delta +1)\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting \(\varepsilon\) that shrinks with \(\Delta\), does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) mixing for the Metropolis chain when \(q\ge (1+\delta )\Delta , \Delta\) is sufficiently large in terms of fixed \(\delta >0\), and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap \(\Omega _{\delta}(1/n)\) and mixing time \(O_{\delta}(n^{2} \log  q+n \log (1/\varepsilon ))\); the sharper \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of \(\delta\). Both the girth restriction and the dependence on \(\delta\) matter. Taking \(\delta =2/\Delta\) is not justified by a theorem that first fixes \(\delta\) and then requires sufficiently large \(\Delta\).

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained \(\Delta +2\) conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.

cards.title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
cards.why: A general guarantee for a basic sampler that preserves individual degrees, with applications to network and fixed-margin statistical models. The reported solution would close the gap between eventual convergence and a uniform polynomial sampling bound.

cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

cards.title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every finite undirected simple graph \(G\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(A(G,\varepsilon)\) halts on every random tape within
\[C\bigl(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\bigr]\ge\frac34?\]
Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of perfect matchings, \(L\) is the complete input bit length defined below, and, whenever \(Z(G)=0\), every run must output zero. This is the existence question for a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme on general unweighted graphs.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge0\), a graph has labeled vertex set \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and an arbitrary subset of the unordered pairs of distinct vertices as its edges. It has no loops, parallel edges or weights. A matching is a subset of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints; it is perfect when every vertex is incident to exactly one of its edges. Each such edge set is counted once, regardless of order or orientation. Thus \(Z(G)\in\mathbb N\), an odd-order graph has count zero, and the empty graph has count one, from its empty matching. The domain includes disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles and arbitrarily large degrees, with no bipartiteness, density, planarity, expansion, or existence promise.

Use the following explicit finite encoding. The graph is encoded by \(1^{n}0\) followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order. This includes the full vertex set even when there are no edges and is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. Write \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms with integers \(0<r<s\). Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Append \(E(r)E(s)\) to the graph encoding. The total length is \(L\); the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\), not just the length of its encoding, may enter the time bound. The output has the form \(E(u)E(v)\) with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), meaning \(\widehat Z=u/v\); reduction to lowest terms is not required.

An algorithm is one finite multitape probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, and an output tape. Each ordinary transition and each newly requested independent fair bit costs one step. Its probability space is the infinite product of fair bits, and the clock bound must hold on every tape for every valid input. Reading, arithmetic, storage operations and writing the whole rational output are all charged. There is no advice, oracle, nonuniform dependence on the graph or accuracy, or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers. No guarantee is needed on malformed inputs. The same \(A,C,k\) must work for all graphs and all valid accuracies; success is per input and is not an average over a graph distribution.

The estimate has relative multiplicative error. In particular, an additive error guarantee on the raw count or on its logarithm is a different condition. Requiring deterministic zero output when no perfect matching exists is a harmless normalization of the usual FPRAS question because perfect-matching existence on general graphs is deterministically decidable in polynomial time. The probability \(3/4\) is fixed, and no random output is required to be an actual matching. This card asks whether the approximation algorithm exists; it does not ask for the numerical value of a fixed graph’s count at the catalogue’s default absolute tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition above or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,k\), and prove its every-random-tape clock, output encoding, exact zero behavior and per-input relative-error probability for every graph and rational accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm and every such polynomial bound; it need not consist of a single finite counterexample graph. Failure or slow mixing of a particular algorithm family does not prove that negation. A conditional impossibility theorem is only a conditional result unless its hypothesis is also proved. Exact exponential-time counting, constant-factor approximation without arbitrary requested accuracy, algorithms only for bipartite or dense graphs, and approximation of the total number of all matchings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Finding a perfect matching is possible in deterministic polynomial time on general graphs, but exact counting is #P-complete even on bipartite graphs. A relative approximation can be much easier than exact counting, as the permanent demonstrates. This question asks whether that distinction persists on all simple graphs, making it one of the central missing cases in the theory of randomized approximate counting.

For an \(m\times m\) nonnegative matrix \(B\), its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_{m}\) is the set of permutations. When \(B\) is a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings between the two specified vertex classes. Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda prove an FPRAS for every nonnegative permanent, solving the bipartite matching case. Their theorem does not require the matrix entries to be strictly positive.

For a general graph on an even number of vertices, the corresponding expression is the hafnian of its symmetric adjacency matrix: the sum, over partitions of the vertices into unordered pairs, of the product of the selected entries. It is different from the permanent of that same square matrix. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine, because the latter also counts directed cycle covers. This example identifies the mathematical distinction between the two targets.

Jerrum and Sinclair’s 1989 Corollary 4.5 gives an FPRAS for the number of matchings of all sizes in arbitrary unweighted graphs. The related weighted monomer–dimer statement has a weight-encoding qualification; no unrestricted binary-weight theorem is needed here. Total matching count can differ exponentially from perfect-matching count: a disjoint union of \(j\) edges has \(2^{j}\) matchings but only one perfect matching. Thus the two quantities are not interchangeable even on elementary graphs.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes identify a precise obstruction for a family of chains on perfect and near-perfect matchings. A near-perfect matching leaves exactly two vertices uncovered, and its hole pattern records those vertices. For the specified JSV-type transitions and any weighting depending only on the hole pattern, their Theorem 2.2 gives graphs on which either perfect matchings have exponentially small stationary probability or the mixing time is exponential. The disjunction matters: the theorem does not assert slow mixing for every weighting, nor impossibility of every FPRAS. Their positive result treats bounded ear complexity of factor-critical subgraphs; a factor-critical graph remains perfectly matchable after deleting any one vertex, and ear count is not its vertex count.

The relevance extends to statistical counting models. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s Proposition 1.2 recalls that, for fixed rational equal interaction parameters \(\beta=\gamma<-1\), approximation of the corresponding two-state spin partition function is equivalent to general perfect-matching approximation under reductions preserving the existence of an FPRAS. The source states this equivalence in both directions and explicitly identifies the perfect-matching question as open. Its other tractable parameter regimes therefore do not settle this one.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s preprint of 27 August 2026 reports an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(m\times m\) zero–one matrix with \(m\ge2\), its Theorem 1 states time \(O(m^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}m\log(2/\delta))\) for relative error \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\); the trivial and zero-permanent cases are handled separately. The state space remains bipartite. This is a reported preprint running-time improvement within the solved neighboring case, not a general-graph theorem; its full proof and bit-level implementation were not independently verified here.

Zihong Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic approximation scheme for weighted hafnians when the support graph has minimum degree at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) and nonzero weights lie in \([\theta,1]\), for fixed \(\gamma>0\) and \(\theta>0\). The unweighted case takes \(\theta=1\), but it still has the fixed density margin. The polynomial’s exponents depend on these fixed margins. The paper explicitly retains the general nonbipartite FPRAS question as open and separately discusses its limitations at the exact Dirac threshold. The reviewed statement does not cover every graph, and the full new proof has not been independently verified.

A positive answer would extend a landmark success of randomized counting beyond bipartiteness. A negative answer would establish a separation between the ease of finding these objects and the existence of arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number. The source-specific Markov-chain obstruction explains part of the difficulty without deciding this algorithm-independent question.

cards.title: FPRAS for #BIS
cards.formal: Does \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\), counting all independent sets in an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Precisely, do there exist one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,k\geq1\) such that, for every encoded bipartite graph \(G\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the machine outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) within \(C(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)^k\) steps on every random tape and satisfies \[\Pr\big[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\leq\widehat Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\big]\geq\tfrac34?\] Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of independent vertex subsets, \(L\) is the complete encoded input length, and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair coin bits.
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\geq0\), the vertex set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), partitioned into disjoint specified sets \(U,V\), either of which may be empty. An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices with one endpoint in each part; there are no loops or parallel edges. An independent set is a subset \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) that contains no complete edge, and \(Z(G)=|\{I\subseteq U\cup V:I\text{ is independent}\}|\). Every independent set is counted once, with weight one, irrespective of its size or the number of its vertices in either part. The empty set is included, so \(Z(G)\geq1\), and the graph with no vertices has \(Z(G)=1\). Graphs may be disconnected and have isolated vertices, arbitrary degrees and parts of unequal sizes. Fix the following explicit finite-alphabet encoding. Write bin(j) for the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer j, with no leading zeros except in bin(0). An input is the string bin(n)#b#a#bin(r)#bin(s), where b has exactly n bits specifying part membership, a has exactly n(n−1)/2 bits specifying adjacency for pairs (i,j), i<j, in increasing lexicographic order, and integers r,s satisfy 0<r<s. Every adjacency bit equal to one must join vertices whose membership bits differ. The accuracy is \(\varepsilon=r/s\); the fraction need not be reduced. Thus isolated vertices are represented explicitly, and L counts all bits and separators, including both accuracy integers. The ceiling \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\) is taken after real division. An output encodes \(\widehat Z=p/q\) as bin(p)#bin(q), with integers \(p\geq0\), \(q\geq1\). The machine has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, with a stream of independent unbiased random bits. All input reading, bit computation, random-bit access and output writing are charged as Turing-machine steps; exact arithmetic on unbounded integers or reals is not a unit-cost operation. There is no oracle, advice, quantum resource or random input-graph assumption. The same program and constants C,k must work for all graph sizes, degrees, bipartitions and accuracies. Malformed strings are rejected by returning 0/1 within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps on every random tape, after increasing the common constants if needed. Deterministic algorithms are permitted as the special case that ignores the random bits.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a single algorithm and constants C,k meet the stated worst-case bit-cost bound, rational-output requirement and per-instance relative-error guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The negative direction must rule out every uniform fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme. Equivalently, every candidate satisfying the polynomial runtime and output conditions must have some valid input \((G,\varepsilon)\) on which its probability of a correct relative approximation is strictly less than \(3/4\). Showing a failure of a particular sampler, a finite running-time lower bound, or difficulty of exact counting does not establish this universal impossibility. A conditional lower bound, for example one assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), is not an unconditional negative resolution unless the assumed separation is also proved. The positive direction must cover every input graph and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with a polynomial degree independent of those inputs; expected runtime alone does not match the specified bound without a proof yielding the required always-bounded scheme. The target is existence of an approximation algorithm with its requested accuracy parameter, so a fixed numerical tolerance of 1/100 does not replace the quantified relative-error requirement. A deterministic fully polynomial scheme would meet the target, but is not required.
cards.why: The canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting: many counting problems share its approximation difficulty, while exact counting hardness does not settle whether a randomized relative approximation is efficient. A general scheme would transfer to problems reducible to it with preserved approximation guarantees; an impossibility proof would separate this central family from the counting problems with known fully polynomial schemes.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.
