cards.context:
Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These user-approved targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
cards.definitions: There are \(m\ge 1\) distinct indivisible items and \(n\ge 1\) bidders. Bidder i privately knows \(v_{i}:2^{[m]}\to Q_{\ge 0}\), with \(v_{i}(\varnothing )=0, v_{i}(S)\le v_{i}(T)\) for \(S\subseteq T\), and \(v_{i}(S)+v_{i}(T)\ge v_{i}(S\cup T)+v_{i}(S\cap T)\) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer \(B\ge 1\) bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most \(\mathrm{P}(n,m,B)\) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles \(S_{1},\ldots ,S_{n}\) and rational payments \(p_{1},\ldots ,p_{n}\); unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, \(u_{i}=v_{i}(S_{i})- p_{i}\). There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type \(v_{i},v_{i}'\), and every \(v_{- i}, v_{i}(S_{i}(v_{i},v_{- i};r))- p_{i}(v_{i},v_{- i};r)\ge v_{i}(S_{i}(v_{i}' ,v_{- i};r))- p_{i}(v_{i}' ,v_{- i};r)\). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=\(\max  \sum_{i} v_{i}(T_{i})\), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint \(T_{i}\subseteq [m]\). The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.

cards.status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. Theorem 2 of the SODA 2021 paper supplies \(O((\log  \log  m)^{2})\) for submodular bidders. The 2026 graph-auction results impose eligibility restrictions. context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected \(O((\log  \log  m)^{3})\) approximation using \(O(n)\) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to \(O((\log  \log  m)^{2})\), while obtaining \(O((\log  \log  m)^{3})\) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

cards.why: Asks whether an indivisible allocation can always control every agent’s envy after the removal of any positively valued good, while distributing all goods. It tests a stronger fairness guarantee than EF1 even before imposing computational efficiency.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.
cards.why: The permanent and determinant have almost identical permutation formulas, but the determinant is a basic efficiently computable polynomial whereas the permanent encodes algebraic counting. This conjecture asks whether enlarging the matrix and changing all its entries to affine forms can bridge that difference at polynomial cost. A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude an entire central model of algebraic computation, including polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas.

context_blocks.text: The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.context:
The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.

benchmark_focus.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
cards.definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every run on a valid input. An unsuccessful run may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

Use one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite description independent of all input parameters. Its tapes have a fixed finite alphabet encoding bits. Each transition can read and write only a fixed number of cells and move each head by at most one cell. An additional instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit at unit cost. This describes ordinary uniform classical bit computation, with no advice, oracle, quantum operations, uncharged preprocessing or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. All reading, writing, arithmetic, memory manipulation and random-bit generation count toward the bound. The output uses the integer encoding specified above, and every bit written is charged.

For a given valid input, randomness is the product measure of independent uniform bits on an infinite random tape; the polynomial clock ensures that only finitely many are read. The success event is the displayed norm inequality, separately for every input. All runs, including those outside that event, must return a valid nonzero integer vector within the same clock. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as the special case that uses no random bits. Expected polynomial time alone is not the stated requirement.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,k,A\;\forall d,n,B\), with both the probability guarantee and the all-run clock imposed after choosing the input. In particular, \(C\) may be large but must be fixed. The factor is \(n^C\), determined by lattice rank; it is not a polynomial in the ambient dimension, the coefficient magnitude or the input bit length. In rank one it is exactly one. There is no input-distribution, shortest-vector uniqueness, ideal-lattice, conditioning, modular or basis-quality promise. The problem concerns arbitrary finite rational bases, including ones with very large coefficients.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and constants meeting every requirement, or of the logical negation of that existence statement. A negative answer must rule out every fixed exponent \(C>0\) and every permitted randomized polynomial-time algorithm, rather than only a deterministic algorithm or a selected small approximation factor. A positive answer must establish the actual nonzero-vector output, success on each basis and all-run bit clock, including coefficient and output lengths. A conditional complexity lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is proved. A gap-decision certificate, a factor depending without a rank bound on the input basis, a uniqueness-promised result, an oracle-call bound excluding subroutine time, or a quantum algorithm alone does not settle this classical search target. No additional numerical tolerance weakens this exact existence proposition.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient classical computation can find short vectors in every Euclidean lattice with a loss bounded by one fixed power of rank. The gap between known general algorithms and this regime is a basic obstacle in lattice complexity. Resolving it would clarify the relation between lattice geometry, efficient approximation and worst-case hardness assumptions used in cryptography; its consequences for particular schemes still depend on the exact problem and parameters.

importance.reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.text: For integer \(M\geq1\), the basis columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\) are both long but their lattice contains \((1,0)\). Thus input column lengths alone do not determine the shortest lattice length. More generally, the same lattice has many bases, and the guarantee must be relative to its intrinsic minimum on every supplied basis.

With its standard parameter, LLL gives a nonzero vector of length at most \(2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1\) in polynomial bit time. The original paper separately controls the number of arithmetic operations and the binary lengths of their operands. Its approximation factor is exponential in rank even though the running time is polynomial; a runtime statement alone does not specify the quality of the vector.

Bennett’s 2023 survey summarizes improved general polynomial-time guarantees with factor \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\). This established upper guarantee is still much larger than any fixed polynomial in rank. It does not prove that every algorithm must lose that much: whether the guarantee can be improved to some \(n^C\) is the existence question on this card.

Haviv and Regev prove hardness at factors \(2^{(\log n)^{1-\varepsilon}}\), for fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unless NP has one-sided-error randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Under the stronger randomized subexponential-time assumption they obtain \(n^{c/\log\log n}\) for some fixed \(c>0\). Both factors are subpolynomial: for every fixed \(C>0\), they eventually lie below \(n^C\). Their theorem therefore does not rule out the looser approximation asked for here. The randomness assumptions are part of the result.

For \(\gamma\geq1\), GapSVP asks whether \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), promised one of those alternatives and given \(r>0\). Aharonov and Regev place this decision problem, for some factor \(\gamma=c\sqrt n\), in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): each promised answer has a polynomial-length certificate verifiable in polynomial time. This is not a polynomial-time method of finding the requested vector. Their full Corollary 1.2 specifies a constant \(c\); it does not assert the result for every smaller factor hidden in big-O notation.

Bennett’s separate search-to-decision question underscores that approximate search SVP, gap decision, unique-SVP and shortest-independent-vectors problems must be distinguished. Cryptographic worst-case-to-average-case reductions concern specified variants at specified approximation and noise parameters. An algorithm here would change the search-SVP landscape; a security reduction alone does not make every cryptographic problem equivalent to it.

Shenoy’s 2024 article advertises an approximation expressed through \(1/(1-\delta)\). In the checked accepted manuscript, Theorem IV.2 defines \(\delta\) from the actual basis, and Corollary IV.3 retains that dependence in a squared-length bound. Merely knowing \(0\leq\delta<1\) supplies no fixed rank-polynomial upper bound on the factor. The manuscript is not counted as a solution of this card; its general convergence claim was not independently verified.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 theorem bounds the number of calls to PotENUM by a quantity polynomial in rank and input coefficient bit length for a fixed reduction parameter. The full Theorem 2 and Remark 2 separately retain an exponential-in-blocksize enumeration factor and the cost of processing each enumeration node. A polynomial number of calls is therefore not a polynomial total bit-time guarantee with arbitrary blocksize.

Hair and Sahai’s April 2026 revision gives a deterministic subexponential-time reduction from satisfiability to Euclidean GapSVP with a subpolynomial approximation gap. Its deterministic hardness conclusion assumes that NP is not contained in the intersection of deterministic time classes \(\operatorname{DTIME}(\exp(m^\eta))\) over all fixed \(\eta>0\), where \(m\) is the source input length. A deterministic reduction does not remove the stated complexity assumption, nor automatically exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under that same deterministic assumption.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s paper, published at RANDOM on September 9, 2026, obtains deterministic constant-factor Euclidean hardness under an explicit lower-bound assumption against nondeterministic circuits. Its parameterized results use another resource measure. Wan’s September 8 revision separately claims unconditional deterministic reductions for every fixed constant factor, but explicitly removes its first version’s dimension-dependent claims after identifying a false tensor-product premise. Neither statement gives unconditional impossibility for all randomized algorithms and all polynomial factors. The new proofs were not independently verified.

The September Wan revision is the version used here: its Theorem 1.2 concerns fixed constant factors, and its introduction expressly withdraws the earlier dimension-dependent consequences. An older abstract or first-version summary must not be used to restore those withdrawn consequences.

Joglekar, Shinde and Agarkar’s September 9 revision concerns a generic metric supplied through a black-box distance oracle, for small constant approximation factors. Its adversary is permitted to perturb the metric. That is distinct from the explicit rational basis and fixed Euclidean norm on this card, and is not an unconditional lower bound for this target.

A classical algorithm satisfying this card also qualifies for the quantum approximation target TCS-7234. The converse is not automatic. Exact quantum search is separately retained as TCS-7169. The present target permits any fixed approximation exponent, rather than asking to optimize that exponent or requiring exact shortest-vector recovery.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
cards.definitions:
All five parameters are finite real numbers and remain fixed as block length grows. Negative, zero, and positive gains are included; powers may be zero or arbitrarily large. The two direct gains and the noise variances are normalized to one. For every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and time \(t\), the noise \(Z_{i,t}\) has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-z^{2}/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All these noises are mutually independent and independent of both messages. There is no fading, channel state, or additional channel memory. Channel parameters and both codebooks are known to all terminals.

For a positive integer \(K\), let \([K]=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\). An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code has \(n,K_{1},K_{2}\ge1\), two independent uniform messages \(M_{i}\in[K_{i}]\), deterministic encoders \(f_{i}:[K_{i}]\to\mathbb R^{n}\), and Borel-measurable decoders \(d_{i}:\mathbb R^{n}\to[K_{i}]\). Transmitter \(i\) sends \(X_{i}^{n}=f_{i}(M_{i})\), and receiver \(i\) estimates only its own message using \(d_{i}(Y_{i}^{n})\). Each code must satisfy
\[\frac{1}{nK_{i}}\sum_{m\in[K_{i}]}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{i}(m)_{t}^{2}\le P_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
This is a separate power budget for each transmitter, averaged over messages and time. It is not a bound on every symbol or every individual codeword, and power cannot be transferred between transmitters. The error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y_{1}^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Y_{2}^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
averaged over the independent uniform messages and all Gaussian noise. There is no maximal-error-over-messages requirement. The encoders may depend arbitrarily on time and their own messages, with arbitrary real codeword entries and no computation bound. They have no shared random seed, common message, feedback, or communication link; neither encoder knows the other message. The receivers cannot communicate. Predetermined time sharing, unequal powers in different phases, and arbitrary temporal dependence within each codeword are allowed subject to the displayed average budgets. There is no secrecy or prescribed signaling-distribution constraint.

All rate logarithms have base two. A nonnegative rate pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a code for each integer block length \(n\ge1\), with message sizes \(K_{i,n}\), such that \(P_{e,n}\to0\) and
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}K_{i,n}}{n}\ge R_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
The region \(C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})\) is the Euclidean closure of all achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\), where \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\); hence \(F\) is finite. These are bits per one real scalar channel use, not per complex channel use. No finite block code must attain a boundary rate. The weights include both endpoints, and the exact supporting function determines the closed region. The task has real mathematical parameters; it does not silently restrict them or the codebooks to rational encodings.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^{2}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\times[0,1]\) and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every tuple in this domain,
\[|g(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)-F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must justify both sides of this error against the operational code definition, using its average-power and average-error conventions and bits per real use. Certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by their midpoint. An exact function also qualifies. A formula or another unambiguous mathematical description may be used; no single-letter syntax, fixed number of auxiliary variables, polynomial evaluation bound, or finite encoding of arbitrary real inputs is required. Any proposed evaluation rule must have a proved meaning and the stated guarantee on the full real domain. An unevaluated restatement of the capacity optimization or its limiting code definition, a sampled plot, and bounds with an unclosed gap do not determine the answer. Sum capacity alone, a restricted signaling optimum, a special interference regime, or an asymptotic high-power approximation is insufficient. The fixed tolerance does not assert an exact capacity theorem.
cards.why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

importance.reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.

progress.text: Strong-interference capacity and the Han–Kobayashi achievable region establish fundamental benchmarks; later exact sum-rate results cover additional regimes without giving every rate tradeoff.
The checked v2 of Etkin–Tse–Wang states and proves the universal one-bit approximation in its complex-channel formulation; the journal version appeared in 2008.
Huleihel–Merhav withdraw the preprint originally used in this card’s provenance, acknowledging that Gaussian memory does not improve the power-controlled comparison region.
Nair–Ng’s published temporal-correlation invariance theorem concerns the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region with time sharing.
Nair–Zhao establish a parameter condition removing multiplexing from an optimized Gaussian Z-channel inner region.
Nair–Zhao give restricted Gaussian-suboptimality examples without power control and retain the full power-controlled Gaussian-capacity conjecture.
Gohari–Nair–Zhao present an auxiliary-receiver outer bound; its full Gaussian specialization gives the stated very-weak-interference and one-sided conclusions.
Khandani v12 claims weak-interference capacity optimality of Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling. The complete proof has not been independently validated in this review.

cards.status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026; retained as uncertain. Khandani 2501.14941v12, dated 7 September 2026, claims Gaussian Han–Kobayashi optimality for weak interference. The current primary PDF’s statement and §§7–8 were read, but its full proof for unrestricted codes was not independently validated; the scope is not an all-real-parameter capacity function. Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and proves only a restricted single-phase Gaussian-suboptimality result without power control, not a refutation of v12 or of the full power-controlled region. Other checked 2025–2026 work supplies special inner-region and outer-bound results. The original Huleihel–Merhav reference was withdrawn in April 2018. Bounded later-work checks found no verified full answer at this card’s 1/100 tolerance; dated discussion of exact capacity alone is not a certification that this numerical benchmark is unsolved.

context_blocks.text: Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. Sections 7–8 present the claimed converse and optimality conclusion. This review checked that statement and scope but did not establish the correctness of the full proof for unrestricted codes. Nair–Zhao’s January criticism predates this revision and is not automatically a refutation of it. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

The user explicitly restored this real-parameter supporting-function target on 12 September 2026. The present review retains its full domain, average-power convention, and absolute \(1/100\) numerical acceptance. It does not add a requirement for a particular finite-letter characterization, and it does not infer fixed-tolerance unsolvability from sources discussing exact capacity.

cards.context:
Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. Sections 7–8 present the claimed converse and optimality conclusion. This review checked that statement and scope but did not establish the correctness of the full proof for unrestricted codes. Nair–Zhao’s January criticism predates this revision and is not automatically a refutation of it. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

The user explicitly restored this real-parameter supporting-function target on 12 September 2026. The present review retains its full domain, average-power convention, and absolute \(1/100\) numerical acceptance. It does not add a requirement for a particular finite-letter characterization, and it does not infer fixed-tolerance unsolvability from sources discussing exact capacity.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal: Determine \(R_{2}(\delta )=\limsup _{n}\to \infty  (1/n)\log _{2} A_{2}(n,\lceil \delta n\rceil )\) for every fixed real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), where \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
cards.definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\); it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance \(d_{H}(x,y)\) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require \(d_{H}(x,y)\ge d\) for every pair of distinct codewords \(x,y\in C; a\) singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate \((\log _{2}|C|)/n\), measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance \(d/n\). The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. \(\delta\) is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is \(h_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\), with \(0 \log _{2}0=0\). The endpoint regimes are known: \(R_{2}(0)=1\) and \(R_{2}(\delta )=0\) for \(1/2\le \delta \le 1\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{2}(\delta )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve. For a lower bound \(\ell\)\((\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) arbitrarily large n admit codes of rate at least \(\ell\)\((\delta )- \varepsilon\) with distance at least \(\lceil \delta n\rceil\); for an upper bound \(u(\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) all sufficiently large n admit no such code of rate greater than \(u(\delta )+\varepsilon\). The proposed g must lie within \(1/100\) of the true rate throughout the domain, and polynomial-time construction or decoding is not required.
cards.why: The basic unresolved packing limit for reliable binary information. An exact answer would identify how much redundancy is intrinsically necessary for a prescribed worst-case separation, independently of algorithmic or algebraic restrictions on the code.

importance.reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.
