context_blocks.text: A binary code represents messages by selected bit strings. Keeping codewords far apart lets a receiver distinguish them after errors, while selecting many codewords increases the amount of information carried by each transmitted block. The rate–distance function asks for the best possible compromise, allowing every conceivable code. It is therefore an information-theoretic limit that must be understood before asking how efficiently an optimal code can be built or decoded.

For a small example, the repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, so it corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The full set of eight three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, so it cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. Generally, disjoint Hamming balls of radius t around codewords are necessary and sufficient for unique correction of every pattern of at most t errors; this requires minimum distance at least \(2t+1\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees \(R_{2}(\delta )\ge 1- h_{2}(\delta )\). A maximal distance-d code covers the cube by balls of radius \(d- 1\), because otherwise another codeword could be inserted. Comparing the cube’s size with the volume of these balls gives the lower bound. In contrast, disjoint balls of radius roughly \(d/2\) give the elementary Hamming upper bound \(1- h_{2}(\delta /2)\). The different radii create a genuine asymptotic gap.

McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch’s 1977 linear-programming bounds greatly sharpen the converse. The first gives \(R_{2}(\delta )\le h_{2}(1/2- \sqrt{\delta (1- \delta )})\); the second also uses constant-weight restrictions and is never weaker. The argument constrains a code’s distribution of pairwise distances through positivity relations, extracting information that a volume count loses. These were the long-standing general benchmarks, but they are no longer the strongest reported bounds after August 2026.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s August 2026 preprint uses classical-input, quantum-output channels to prove stronger bounds for classical binary codes, including nonlinear codes. Mixed-qubit channels strictly improve the first MRRW bound, and a masked version strictly improves the second throughout \(0<\delta <1/2\). Quantum states enter the converse proof as an analytical tool; the codes whose sizes are bounded still consist of ordinary bit strings. The result narrows the gap without matching the Gilbert–Varshamov lower curve.

Barg’s September 2026 note explains the relationship between this channel argument and a concurrent Delsarte-certificate proof. For the improvement of the first bound, he shows that the two variational expressions coincide. The geometric change is to associate a moving subspace, rather than a single vector, with each codeword, allowing a stronger packing argument. This provides a further derivation and interpretation of the new bound; it does not establish the exact rate function.

Lower-bound improvements require equally careful interpretation. Jiang and Vardy improve the finite-length Gilbert bound by a factor proportional to n in the fixed-distance regime they cover. Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a concise probabilistic proof of a square-root-n improvement for linear codes and extends the method to quantum codes; the classical square-root factor had predecessors. After taking \(\log _{2}\) and dividing by n, any polynomial multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log  n/n)\). Such refinements do not increase the leading rate exponent.

Changing the error model also changes the answer. Capacity for independent random bit flips and capacity for list decoding are not the same quantity as the largest rate at a prescribed minimum distance. This card asks about worst-case pairwise separation with unrestricted binary codes. It also does not transfer improvements for sufficiently large alphabets directly to binary codes: changing alphabet and concatenating codes changes their rate and distance parameters.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

importance.reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.

progress.text: Alon–Shapira establish general one-sided hereditary graph testability; the guarantee is qualitative and does not give polynomial sample bounds for every family.
Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability of cographs, or induced-four-vertex-path freeness. Their path notation counts edges.
Gishboliner–Shapira establish the checked finite-family sufficient and necessary conditions, including examples showing that they do not coincide.
The checked author revision and Combinatorica publication give a single-exponential induced-four-cycle bound and state the polynomial conjecture separately.
The survey states the finite-family structural classification as Problem 3.14, with the four-cycle as the first key open case.
The ECCC container characterization provides explicit tester/container parameter conversions. No total classifier from an arbitrary finite forbidden list is established in its inspected main results.

context_blocks.text: Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

progress.text: Fischer–Newman establish that dense-graph testability implies distance estimability. The journal publication is in 2007, following STOC 2005.
Fiat–Ron give polynomial-query distance approximation for induced P3-freeness, induced P4-freeness and chordality; their induced C4 result has exponential reciprocal-accuracy dependence.
Gishboliner–Kushnir–Shapira improve the general and hereditary conversion bounds. Theorem 1.9 still has a double-exponential loss and does not prove polynomial preservation.
The survey records the stronger quantitative conversion as Problem 5.4 and describes positive special cases after it.

context_blocks.text: A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
cards.formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most \(1/10\) and confidence at least \(9/10\), while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
cards.why: The problem seeks a privacy analogue of a foundational characterization theorem in learning theory.

progress.text: The survey gives lower bound $\Omega(\mathrm{VC}+\log^*\mathrm{LD})$ and upper bound $\min\{O(\log|C|),\widetilde O(\mathrm{LD}^5)\}$. The $\mathrm{VC}=1$ case is nearly understood; the general gap remains.

references.title: Invited Open Problem: Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?
references.authors: Kobbi Nissim; Uri Stemmer; Eliad Tsfadia
references.locator: Open Questions 1–2; Theorems 2–3

cards.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
cards.review_note: Concrete specialization of the quantitative target following Open Question 1: accuracy, confidence, epsilon, delta, and the meaning of polynomial overhead are fixed explicitly. The survey itself suppresses these parameters. Importance is editorial; cited proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

cards.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to \(\{0,1\}\). \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. \(LD(C)\) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{X}\) of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target \(h\in C\) and distribution D on X, with probability at least \(9/10\) over m independent draws \(x_{i}\) from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most \(1/10\). Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector \((h(x))_{h\in C}\) can be identified, giving at most \(2^{|}C|\) cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.

cards.title: Optimal error for pure-DP continual counting
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(T\to \infty , E(T)=\inf _{M} \max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{T}} E_{Y\sim M_{x}}[\max _{1\le t\le T}|Y_{t}- \sum_{i=1}^{t} x_{i}|]\), where the infimum is over all causal \((1/2,0)\)-differentially private mechanisms defined below.
cards.why: Determines the minimax cost of repeatedly publishing a running count while protecting each individual event under pure privacy. It separates guarantees for the whole observed trajectory from per-time or average accuracy.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.

context_blocks.text: Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream \((1,0,1,1)\), the exact outputs are \((1,1,2,3)\). Changing its second bit gives \((1,1,1,1)\) and exact outputs \((1,2,3,4)\): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only \(1/T\). This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is \(O(\log ^{2}T)\). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for \(E(T)\) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.

cards.answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.

importance.reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.

progress.text: Bulatov proves the ordinary finite-template CSP dichotomy, covering the special case \(A=B\).
Zhuk independently proves the same ordinary CSP dichotomy; the final arXiv revision is dated 2 October 2020.

The published Krokhin–Vagnozzi theorem proves NP-hardness for \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) and completes the three-element symmetric ternary target classification for approximations of exactly-one satisfaction.

cards.status_note: An open general classification question in the 2022 survey and the published July 2026 Krokhin–Vagnozzi article. The latter resolves a restricted three-element target family; the May 2026 Promise MMSNP preprint gives a logical correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full unconditional finite-pair dichotomy or counterexample. Individual theorem statements and scopes were checked, but their full proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal: For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous structure A over a finite relational signature, and every finite-signature first-order reduct B of A, is \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) either decidable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed finite arities. A is homogeneous if every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of A. It is finitely bounded if there is a finite set F of finite structures in its signature such that a finite structure embeds into A exactly when none of the structures in F embeds into it; embeddings preserve both relations and their complements. Countable allows finite or countably infinite domains. B has the same domain as A, with finitely many relations each definable by a first-order formula over A without parameters; it may forget original relations and introduce definable ones. For each fixed B, an input to \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) is an explicitly encoded finite structure I in B’s signature. Accept exactly when there is a map h from the domain of I to that of B preserving every relation tuple. Equivalently, a finite conjunction of atomic B-constraints must have a satisfying assignment. h need not be injective. A, B and their defining formulas are fixed, not part of the input; running times are measured in the finite instance’s bit length. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a Turing machine that halts on every finite input consisting of a system of word equations \(U_{i}=V_{i}\) and a system of integer linear equalities and inequalities on the variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when a simultaneous solution exists in the free monoid \(\Sigma\)*? The alphabet, equations, variables, and arithmetic coefficients are part of the input, with the conventions below.
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet of constant symbols and \(X=\{X_{1},\ldots ,X_{k}\}\) is a disjoint finite set of variables. Each \(U_{i},V_{i}\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma \cup X\); repeated occurrences of a variable must receive the same substitution. A solution assigns a finite word \(\sigma (X_{j})\in \Sigma\)* to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing every letter of \(\Sigma\). The empty word is allowed. Every substituted equality \(\sigma (U_{i})=\sigma (V_{i})\) must hold as a literal equality of words. The additional constraints are a finite conjunction of atoms \(\sum _{j} a_{j}|\sigma (X_{j})|\le b\) or \(\sum _{j} a_{j}|\sigma (X_{j})|=b\), where all coefficients and constants are signed binary integers. Length is the number of alphabet symbols. There is no product of two variable lengths, letter-frequency counter, regular-expression predicate, string-to-integer conversion, or universal quantifier. The requested decider need not run in polynomial, elementary, or any specified computable time bound, but must terminate on satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs alike. Nonempty-substitution requirements can be imposed using |\(\sigma (X_{j})|\ge 1\). In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The IJCAR 2026 primary source explicitly leaves general word-equation satisfiability with length constraints open. The two-variable quadratic theorem is a restricted case, and the July NEXP-hardness claim is a lower bound rather than a decidability result. This card fixes existential satisfiability with concatenation and integer linear length constraints only.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation \(Xa=bX\) yields the harmless length identity |\(X|+1=1+|X|\). Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality \(a=b\). This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. This strengthens the PP-hardness stated in its first version. Its NEXP-completeness theorem is for arithmetic with divisibility, not for unrestricted word equations with lengths. Positive Boolean formulas can be expanded into finitely many conjunctions for purposes of decidability, but that expansion need not be polynomial. The result therefore records a substantial complexity barrier without establishing a general decider or undecidability.

cards.definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.

context_blocks.text: A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇\(\psi\) is false for every replacement \(\psi\). Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class C of finite simple graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{C}, a\) computable function \(f_{C}:N\to N\) and a constant \(d_{C}\) such that \(A_{C}\) decides whether G satisfies a first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in time \(f_{C}(|\varphi |)(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{C}}\) for every \(G\in C\)? The precise effectiveness condition is given below; the graph is supplied without a structural decomposition.
cards.definitions: The class C is fixed, is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs, and is not part of each input. First-order sentences use equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual vertices. They do not quantify over sets, and no vertex order or arithmetic is supplied. The input is the explicitly represented graph G and the sentence \(\varphi\); the parameter \(k=|\varphi |\) is its encoded length. The algorithm must halt on every input, and its correctness and stated time bound are required when \(G\in C\); it need not recognize membership in C. To define monadic dependence, let \(\theta (x,y)\) be any fixed first-order formula using adjacency and finitely many additional unary predicates. A graph in \(T_{\theta}(G)\) is obtained by interpreting these predicates as arbitrary vertex subsets, putting an edge between distinct u,v whenever \(\theta (u,v)\) or \(\theta (v,u)\) holds, and taking any induced subgraph. C is monadically dependent when no single \(\theta\) gives all finite graphs among the outputs \(T_{\theta}(G), G\in C\). For an explicit effective version, define \(\mathrm{P}_{s}\) as the bipartite powerset graph with vertices \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{s}\) and \(b_{S}\) for every \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,s\}\), and edges \(a_{i} b_{S}\) exactly when \(i\in S\). Require a computable function \(b:N\to N_{\ge 1}\) such that, for every formula \(\theta\) and every \(G\in C, \mathrm{P}_{b(|\theta |)}\) is absent from \(T_{\theta}(G)\). Formula length includes its predicate symbols under a fixed effective encoding. This is the computable dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24. The programs computing b and the eventual algorithm may depend on C; they are not extra per-instance certificates. The exponent \(d_{C}\) is independent of k. The query-evaluation problem here is for the plain graph signature; unary colours occur in the structural definition. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper. The independent-side hardness and stable-side algorithm are known; radius-one merge-width does not provide the full algorithm. This card fixes the effective dependence-function convention to require a computable FPT bound. No resolution found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try \(n^{k}\) choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form \(f(k)n^{d}\): the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{AW}[*]\), this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive \(\eta\), the number of distinct sets \(N(v)\cap A\) is \(O(|A|^{1+\eta})\) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and \(\eta\). It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width \(n^{o(1)}\) in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

A positive answer would unify several major algorithmic graph frameworks through one logical condition and explain when small declarative queries can avoid repeated high-dimensional enumeration. A counterexample satisfying the effective hypothesis would show that the absence of arbitrary logical graph encoding is insufficient for tractability. Either outcome would sharpen the connection between graph structure and query evaluation.

cards.title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with \(O_{q}(N)\) preprocessing and \(O_{q}(1)\) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
cards.definitions: A query is a finite formula \(q(\bar\{x\})=\exists \bar\{y\} \land _{i} R_{i}(\bar\{z\}_{i})\), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain \([n]; N=1+n\)+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in \(O(\log (N+2))\) bits. \(q(D)\) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of \(O_{q}(\log (N+2))\) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants \(C_{q},B_{q}\) whose preprocessing takes at most \(C_{q} N\) steps, whose word length is at most \(B_{q} \log _{2}(N+2)\), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most \(C_{q}\) after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.

context_blocks.text: A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer \((x,z)\), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example \(\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge \(\{x,z\}\) creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query \(R(x,y)\land R(y,z)\land R(x,t)\land R(t,z)\). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with \(t=y\). When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.
